instructions:
Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 672 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool compared the draft with essays that students wrote on other assignments. Use its report when you revise:

Tone check against human essay writing (673 words). Distance from the human centre: 0.4 (1.0 is typical for a human text).
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences: 0.42 (1 = as if words were dealt at random); most human texts are between 0.63 and 1.67. Feeling is spread evenly over the sentences. People bunch it: some sentences are flat, some carry a lot.
Inside the human range: positive charge; negative charge; net charge; total charge, positive plus negative; words that carry charge; charge under a negation; charge after an intensifier such as 'very'; charge after a contrast word such as 'but'; net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean.
These are ranges, not targets. Change wording only where the change also makes the text more specific or more honest.

Draft:

Every student should take part in at least one extracurricular activity. Some people will say that a school cannot force a student to spend time outside of class on something he or she did not choose. I understand that concern, but I agree with the principal's decision. Required participation does not mean forced fun. It means that every student gets a chance to find a place where he or she belongs, and for many students that place is not in a math textbook or a lecture hall.

The most obvious benefit is that activities give students a reason to show up. Many students who struggle in class have a hard time seeing why school matters. When a student joins the track team, the reason to come to school becomes clearer. He has practice after lunch, teammates who expect him there, and a coach who notices when he misses. I have watched a student who barely passed freshman English become the most reliable member of the yearbook staff. She learned to interview classmates, meet deadlines, and fix layouts at eleven at night. Her grades improved because she finally had a reason to care about what she was doing during the day.

Extracurricular activities also teach skills that classrooms rarely cover. Student council, for example, asks students to plan events, raise money, and argue for their ideas in front of adults who may not agree with them. A student who runs a food drive learns how to budget, how to ask for donations without sounding desperate, and how to recover when a plan falls apart. These lessons do not show up on a standardized test, but employers and colleges care about them. Sports teach discipline and how to lose gracefully. Debate teaches a student to listen to the other side before answering. Music ensembles teach that one person's mistake affects everyone in the room.

Some critics argue that students who already have jobs, family responsibilities, or heavy academic loads cannot fit in another commitment. That concern deserves respect, and a good policy should account for it. However, the requirement does not need to be rigid. A student can choose from dozens of options, including clubs that meet once a week or service projects that take a few hours a month. The school can also count volunteer work at a library or community center. The goal is not to fill every afternoon with practice. The goal is to make sure every student has at least one connection to the school beyond the bell schedule.

Opponents also say that a student who is not interested in sports or drama will be made miserable by a required activity. Yet the variety of options makes it unlikely that anyone will find nothing of interest. A student who dislikes competition might enjoy photography, robotics, or the chess club. A student who is shy might find that the gardening club gives him a quiet place to talk with others. Many students discover interests they never knew they had only because someone asked them to try something new. Ask any adult who has a lifelong hobby how it started, and many will say they tried it by accident.

Finally, schools have a responsibility to prepare students for life after graduation, and life is rarely a series of solitary tasks. People work in teams, lead projects, and deal with conflict. Extracurricular activities are a low-stakes place to practice those skills. A student who has spent a season on a team or a year on a committee walks into college or a first job with experience that a transcript alone cannot show.

For these reasons, I believe the principal is right. Requiring at least one activity is not an attempt to control students' free time. It is an invitation to discover something that might change how a student sees school and himself. The policy will not work perfectly for everyone, but it gives every student a door to walk through, and that is worth the small effort it asks of each of them.
